All simulation work in this project is built on [`mizer`](https://sizespectrum.org/mizer/), an open-source R package for size-spectrum modelling of fish communities (Scott, Blanchard & Andersen, 2014). Rather than tracking species as the primary unit, `mizer` tracks the abundance of individuals **by body mass** $w$, with species entering only as a tag carrying a particular set of physiological parameters. This follows from Sheldon, Prakash and Sutcliffe's (1972) observation that marine biomass is distributed roughly evenly across logarithmic body-mass classes, a regularity that holds across species boundaries as well as within them. It is also what makes the traffic analogy at the heart of this project meaningful: body mass plays the role of position on a road, individuals move continuously from small $w$ to large $w$ as they grow, and a "jam" is a pile-up of biomass at a size class rather than a location.

## Governing Equation

`mizer` evolves the abundance density $n(w,t)$ using a McKendrick-von Foerster-type PDE, a continuity equation with a mortality sink term:

$$\frac{\partial n(w,t)}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial}{\partial w}\Big[g(w,t)\,n(w,t)\Big] - \mu(w,t)\,n(w,t)$$

where $g(w,t)$ is individual growth rate (the flux velocity, analogous to $V(x)$ for traffic) and $\mu(w,t)$ is total mortality. The flux term is structurally identical to the traffic-flow equation $\partial_t n = -\partial_x J$ used elsewhere in this project. The extra $-\mu\,n$ term is the key difference: fish can leave the system by dying at any size, not only by exiting at the largest size class, and fishing mortality is one additive component of $\mu(w,t)$, making it the model's primary intervention lever.

## Growth and the Predation Kernel

The non-linearity that makes jamming possible lives inside $g(w,t)$: growth is not assumed as a function of $w$, it is *derived* from how much a fish of mass $w$ actually manages to eat. A predator searches at rate $\gamma w^q$ and encounters prey weighted by a feeding kernel $\phi(w/w_p)$, log-normal in the predator:prey mass ratio and controlled by two parameters used throughout this project's code: $\beta$ (preferred mass ratio) and $\sigma$ (diet breadth). A small $\beta$ or narrow $\sigma$ concentrates a predator's diet on a tight band of prey sizes, precisely the condition Datta, Delius and Law (2011) identify as destabilising for this class of equation.

Encountered food $E(w,t)$ passes through a saturating functional response bounded by a maximum intake rate $h w^n$, giving the **feeding level** $f(w,t) = E/(E + hw^n) \in [0,1]$. Growth is what remains after metabolic cost:

$$g(w,t) = \alpha\, f(w,t)\, h\, w^{n} - k_s\, w^{p}$$

This closes the feedback loop: high local abundance depletes prey, lowering $f$, lowering $g$, so individuals spend longer at that mass, raising local abundance further — the direct analogue of `high density → lower velocity → higher density`, and the mechanism this project is built to probe. A feeding level collapsing toward 0 is exactly the symptom of a size class caught in a jam.

## Mortality and Fishing

Total mortality is $\mu(w,t) = \mu_p(w,t) + \mu_{ext}(w) + F(w,t)$: predation mortality (generated by every other size class's search effort, which couples all size classes and species together), a fixed background term, and fishing mortality $F(w,t) = q \cdot S(w) \cdot E_f$. The selectivity function $S(w)$ encodes gear choice — a hard `knife_edge` cutoff, a smooth `sigmoid_length` ramp, or a dome-shaped `double_sigmoid_length` window — and is the model's representation of the fishing intervention this project tests as a way of relieving, rather than only diminishing, a jam.

## The Background Resource

Growth of the smallest size classes depends on a background resource (standing in for plankton), evolved under semichemostat dynamics:

$$\frac{\partial n_R(w,t)}{\partial t} = r(w)\big[c(w) - n_R(w,t)\big] - \mu_p(w,t)\,n_R(w,t)$$

with replenishment rate $r(w)$ and carrying capacity $c(w) = \kappa w^{-\lambda}$. At quasi-equilibrium, $n_R^*(w) \approx r(w)c(w) / (r(w) + \mu_p(w))$: when $r(w)$ is large, $n_R^* \approx c(w)$ regardless of fish density, decoupling growth from abundance; when $r(w)$ is small, $n_R^*$ becomes acutely sensitive to it, amplifying the feedback loop. This is why `resource_decrease` (this project's own multiplier on $r(w)$) is the primary experimental knob used throughout.

## Reproduction, Multiple Species, and Implementation

A Beverton-Holt density-dependent recruitment function closes the model at its smallest size class, capping recruitment even under high egg production — a stabilising influence this project has directly tested against the destabilising growth feedback above. Although most of this project's exploratory work uses a single calibrated species, `mizer` is natively multi-species: every species shares the same resource pool and predation kernel machinery, coupling species even without an explicit interaction term.

Numerically, `mizer` discretises the weight axis on a log-spaced grid and solves the resulting ODE system forward in time. Integrator choice matters: the default explicit-Euler-style scheme can produce spurious numerical ringing easily mistaken for a real limit cycle, which is why every oscillation reported in this project was re-verified under a more accurate scheme (`predictor_corrector` or `tr_bdf2`) before being trusted. `steadyNewton()` and `projectToSteady()` were used throughout to locate fixed points directly, including unstable ones a forward simulation could never settle onto.

## Why mizer for This Project

`mizer` was chosen over a bespoke solver because the non-local, density-dependent growth feedback this project's hypothesis depends on is not an add-on, it *is* `mizer`'s core mechanism, already implemented and validated against real, calibrated species. This let the project focus on the scientific question rather than re-deriving the underlying growth model. The knobs this project leans on most heavily — `resource_decrease`/`capacity_mult` on $r(w)$ and $c(w)$, $\beta$/$\sigma$ on diet breadth, and gear `sel_func`/`knife_edge_size` on the fishing intervention — are `mizer`'s own native parameterisation of exactly the mechanisms the traffic analogy predicts should matter.
